sources.note: For Lokoya, Lopit and Otuho: 'There are tones (at least High and Low), used for both lexical and grammatical distinctions.. The nominative case is differentiated from the absolutive by a change in the tonal pattern across the noun' (p. 427). Explicitly nothing for Lango or Dongotono: no data.

sources.citation: Billington, Rosey. 2017. The phonetics and phonology of the Lopit language. PhD thesis, School of Languages and Linguistics, University of Melbourne. sources.note: Nothing on Lango; detailed tone analysis is for Lopit only. States: 'In Vossen's analyses, Lopit, Dongotono and Lokoya are considered to be similar enough to group together for a phonology sketch, while Otuho is treated separately'.

sources.citation: Simonse, Simon. 2018 [1st ed. Leiden: Brill 1992]. Kings of Disaster: Dualism, Centralism and the Scapegoat King in Southeastern Sudan. Revised edition (Kampala: Fountain / Michigan State UP). CC BY-ND copy on the Internet Archive. Introduction 'Technical notes: On spelling'; ch. 2 passage on the Lotuho language group (after Ehret 1982) with fn. 7 on 'Lango'; appendix list 'Lango (Dongotono, Logir, Lokwaa, Ketebo, Lorwama, Imotong)'.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: no phonology content: spelling key for Bari-based transcriptions (c, h, o-umlaut, ny, implosive 'b 'd); notes that only Bari has an accepted spelling, Lotuho 'has at least two rival spellings', Lulubo/Lokoya/Pari 'have not been developed for writing'; on the Lango varieties: 'Dongotono, including the dialects of the Imotong, Ketebo, Logir, Lokwa and Lorwama. I am not aware of scholarly research on the relationships between these different dialects.' The words tone/tonal occur only in non-linguistic senses (FTS inside the item: 0 linguistic hits). Useful only as identity evidence and as a poin…
